title: Reading a plan before you apply it
summary: The plan symbols, forces replacement, known after apply, a real plan as a graph, saved plans, plan JSON with jq, and -detailed-exitcode for scripts.

steps.title: The plan is the review
body: Every line of a plan starts with a symbol. Learn them cold:
| Symbol | Meaning | Risk |
| `+` | create | low: new things |
| `~` | update in place | depends on the attribute (a resize may restart a server) |
| `-/+` | destroy, **then** create a replacement | **high**: data and IDs are lost, there is a gap |
| `+/-` | create the replacement first, then destroy (`create_before_destroy`) | high, but no gap |
| `-` | destroy | **high** |
| `<=` | read a data source during apply | none |
Inside a resource, `# forces replacement` marks the attribute that turned an update into a replacement, and
`(known after apply)` marks values nobody can know until the provider creates the object (a new ID, an IP). A value
that becomes *known after apply* also ripples into every resource that references it: they may be replaced too.
Read a plan **bottom-up**: the summary line (`Plan: 3 to add, 1 to change, 3 to destroy.`) first. Any number of
destroys means: find every `-` and `-/+`, and be able to say why each one is fine.

steps.title: A real plan, as a graph
body: This is the real `terraform show -json` of the plan you will make in the next step: a teammate's branch for release
1.5. Dependencies are on the left, what uses them on the right. Click each resource to see its attribute diff.
Look for: the two `-/+` replacements and the attribute that **forces** each one; why `local_file.authorized_keys` is
replaced although nobody touched it (the arrow from the key); the `-` and the reason Terraform gives for it.

steps.prompt: In that plan, why is `local_file.authorized_keys` replaced, when the branch did not change its block?
options: Its `content` references `tls_private_key.deploy.public_key_openssh`, which is *known after apply* because the key is replaced, and a file's content forces replacement
Terraform replaces every file on each apply
steps.explain: Replacing one resource can ripple: everything that reads one of its attributes gets a new value. Here that is harmless; with AWS, replacing a security group or a subnet can replace every instance that references it. The plan card highlights this *blast radius* when you select a replaced resource.

steps.prompt: These come from real AWS provider plans (hashicorp/aws 6.x). Update in place, or replacement?
steps.explain: Rules of thumb: names and identity-like settings (a bucket name, an AMI, encryption chosen at creation) force replacement; sizes, versions and tags usually update in place, although the update itself can mean a restart (an instance type change stops and starts the instance; a major engine upgrade needs `allow_major_version_upgrade`). The plan always tells you: look for `# forces replacement`.

steps.title: Save it, read it as JSON, script it
body: A saved plan is a binary file. Two ways to read it:
```bash
terraform plan -out=review.tfplan
terraform show review.tfplan                 # the same text as plan printed
terraform show -json review.tfplan | jq .    # machine-readable: what CI tools and policy checks read
In the JSON, `.resource_changes[]` has one entry per resource instance with `.address` and `.change.actions`:
`["create"]`, `["update"]`, `["delete"]`, `["no-op"]`, `["read"]`, or two actions for a replacement
(`["delete","create"]`, or `["create","delete"]` with `create_before_destroy`). `.change.replace_paths` lists the
attributes that forced it, and `.action_reason` says why.
```bash
# every address that will be destroyed or replaced
terraform show -json review.tfplan | jq -r '.resource_changes[] | select(.change.actions | index("delete")) | .address'
**`terraform plan -detailed-exitcode`** makes scripts easy: exit **0** = no changes, **1** = error, **2** = there are
changes. A nightly job that runs it and alerts on 2 is a simple drift detector.

steps.title: Review the release branch
prompt: `~/infra/web` is applied from `main`; the branch `feature/release-1.5` is checked out (`git log --oneline`). Review it
2. Write the addresses of every resource that will be **replaced** (destroyed and created again) into
3. Write the addresses of every resource that will only be **destroyed** into `~/answers/destroyed.txt`.
Use `terraform show -json review.tfplan | jq`. Do not apply: this is a review.

checks.name: review.tfplan is a plan of the branch
checks.cmd: cd ~/infra/web && terraform show -json review.tfplan | jq -e '[.resource_changes[] | select(.address == "local_file.robots")] | length == 1' >/dev/null
checks.fail: Save the plan of the checked-out branch with `terraform plan -out=review.tfplan` in `~/infra/web`.

checks.name: replaced.txt lists the replacements
checks.cmd: cd ~/infra/web && diff <(sed '/^$/d' ~/answers/replaced.txt) <(terraform show -json review.tfplan | jq -r '.resource_changes[] | select(.change.actions | length == 2) | .address' | sort)
checks.fail: `~/answers/replaced.txt` should list each replaced address once, sorted (`>` lines are missing, `<` lines should not be there). Replacements have two actions.

checks.name: destroyed.txt lists the plain destroys
checks.cmd: cd ~/infra/web && diff <(sed '/^$/d' ~/answers/destroyed.txt) <(terraform show -json review.tfplan | jq -r '.resource_changes[] | select(.change.actions == ["delete"]) | .address' | sort)
checks.fail: `~/answers/destroyed.txt` should list the addresses whose actions are exactly `["delete"]`.

checks.name: nothing was applied
checks.cmd: cd ~/infra/web && terraform state show -no-color tls_private_key.deploy | grep -q 'algorithm.*"RSA"' && terraform state list | grep -qx local_file.banner
checks.fail: The state changed: this was a review only. Press Reset scenario and do it again without `apply`.

hints: `terraform plan -out=review.tfplan`, then `terraform show -json review.tfplan | jq '.resource_changes[] | {address, actions: .change.actions}'` shows every address with its actions.
A replacement has two actions: `select(.change.actions | length == 2)`. A plain destroy is `select(.change.actions == ["delete"])`.
solution: terraform show -json review.tfplan | jq -r '.resource_changes[] | select(.change.actions | length == 2) | .address' | sort > ~/answers/replaced.txt
terraform show -json review.tfplan | jq -r '.resource_changes[] | select(.change.actions == ["delete"]) | .address' | sort > ~/answers/destroyed.txt
steps.explain: Two replacements (the key, and the file that holds its public key) and one destroy (the banner, *because local_file.banner is not in configuration*). In a real review you would now ask: is replacing the deploy key planned with the team that uses it? That is the conversation a plan is for. The same `jq` lines are the start of a CI check that labels a pull request *destroys resources*.

steps.prompt: A nightly job runs this against production. Last night someone changed a setting by hand in the console, so the plan shows one update. What does it print?
steps.explain: 0 means *no changes*, 1 an error, 2 *changes present*. Without `-detailed-exitcode`, `plan` exits 0 whether or not there are changes. Careful in scripts with `set -e`: exit code 2 stops them, so capture it (`terraform plan -detailed-exitcode || rc=$?`).

steps.prompt: A CI step that fails the pull request when the plan destroys anything. Fill the gaps.
code: if [ "$destroys" -gt 0 ]; then echo "plan destroys $destroys resources: needs a second reviewer"; exit 1; fi
steps.explain: `index("delete")` finds both plain destroys and replacements, because a replacement's actions include `delete`. The JSON calls it `delete`; the text output and the CLI say *destroy*.
